svg.title: Radioiodine-refractory disease: the criteria, and what the trials measured
svg.desc: Schematic in two columns: on the left the criteria for radioiodine-refractory disease, on the right four phase III trials with their numbers of patients, median progression-free survival and hazard ratios. A grey band across the top states that nothing in the left column carries an evidence grade: the two gates are listed by the guideline as good practice, which it does not grade, the criteria themselves sit in the discussion paragraph beneath them and carry no recommendation strength at all, and the guideline says these criteria will go on changing. The first cell on the left holds the two gates, tagged "good practice, which the guideline does not grade": first, a patient who has never had ablative or therapeutic radioiodine cannot be diagnosed as refractory to it, and those who qualify should have it first because that is how the answer is found; second, a patient already judged refractory should not be given empiric radioiodine again, and other treatments are to be considered. The second cell holds the two strong criteria: a lesion visible on imaging or PET with no iodine uptake on the post-therapy scan; or progression within six months of one appropriately dosed radioiodine treatment where the post-therapy scan did show uptake. The third holds the two supportive criteria: no uptake on the diagnostic scan while the lesion is visible on imaging, which predicts a poorer response though some such patients still have a positive post-therapy scan; and uptake in only some lesions, which does not rule radioiodine out but is not enough on its own. A further cell records that refractory does not mean a short time left: the guideline says in the same section that some patients die within three to five years and that others survive a long time with stable or extremely slowly progressive disease, so the first step after "refractory" is often not a drug at all - patients who are asymptomatic, stable or barely progressing, or who carry significant comorbidity, may be imaged every three to twelve months on suppressive thyroid hormone therapy, a conditional recommendation with low certainty. A yellow cell states that the threshold for starting a drug is imaging and not a blood test: the guideline requires visible progression of lesions on imaging before systemic therapy, not a blood curve climbing upwards; a rising thyroglobulin on its own is written down as not constituting a reason to start; and the trials below enrolled people with progression on imaging in the first place. The left column closes with the recommendation to test tumour tissue for biomarkers before systemic therapy starts, strong with moderate certainty, noting that the drugs chosen by genotype work well but rest on very few patients, whose numbers are in the article while this figure carries only the phase III trials. The right column opens with a red cell warning that not every confidence interval is 95%: the hazard ratio 0.21 for lenvatinib is a 99% confidence interval; the response rate in the cabozantinib interim analysis is a 99% confidence interval; the progression-free survival hazard ratio 0.22 for cabozantinib is a 96% confidence interval; and only the hazard ratios in the sorafenib and BRAF phase III trials are 95%. A note adds that when the levels differ the widths of the intervals cannot be read in the same sentence, and that "median progression-free survival not reached" for cabozantinib is the older wording from the interim analysis, the 2022 extended analysis being the one to use. Four trial cards follow, each drawing two bars on the same scale in months, drug above and control below. The lenvatinib phase III enrolled 392 patients with radioiodine-refractory, progressive differentiated thyroid cancer, 261 on drug and 131 on placebo, with median progression-free survival 18.3 months against 3.6 months and a hazard ratio of 0.21 (0.14 to 0.31) tagged as a 99% confidence interval; response was 64.8%, 4 of them complete, against 1.5%, and on overall survival this trial published no overall-survival hazard ratio or test at all, only that median overall survival had not been reached in either arm; discontinuation for adverse events was 14.2% against 2.3%, of 20 deaths during treatment 6 were judged drug-related, and hypertension, diarrhoea, fatigue, loss of appetite and weight loss each exceeded four in ten. The sorafenib phase III enrolled 417 patients, 207 on drug and 210 on placebo, with median progression-free survival 10.8 months against 5.8 and a hazard ratio of 0.59 (0.45 to 0.76) at 95%; overall survival showed no significant difference, hazard ratio 0.80 (0.54 to 1.19), while 71.4% of the placebo arm crossed over to the drug after progressing and the authors write that the overall-survival result may be confounded by it; response was 12.2% (24/196), all partial; dose interruption 66.2%, reduction 64.3%, discontinuation for adverse events 18.8%, and serious adverse events 37.2% against 26.3%. The cabozantinib phase III is given from its 2022 extended analysis: 258 randomised, median follow-up 10.1 months, median progression-free survival 11.0 months against 1.9, hazard ratio 0.22 (0.15 to 0.32) tagged as a 96% confidence interval, with the interval around the median of 11.0 months also 96%, from 7.4 to 13.8; response was 11.0% (95% confidence interval 6.9 to 16.9) against 0, grade 3 or 4 adverse events 62% against 28%, and the overall-survival hazard ratio of 0.76 (0.45 to 1.31) is likewise not significant, the authors writing that crossover will confound future analyses of overall survival; in the interim analysis of 187 patients the response rate was 10/67 among the first 100 randomised (15%, 99% confidence interval 5.8 to 29.3) against 0/33 and did not meet the prespecified threshold for significance. The BRAF phase III read out after the guideline was written: 153 previously treated patients with BRAF V600E-positive, radioiodine-refractory differentiated thyroid cancer, randomised 101 to 52, median progression-free survival 12.8 months against 3.7, stratified hazard ratio 0.38 (0.25 to 0.57) at 95%, with the interval around the median of 12.8 months 10.2 to 21.2 at 95%; response was 57% against 4%; the interim analysis of overall survival has not reached significance, stratified hazard ratio 0.66 (0.36 to 1.19), and that trial is still running; the authors conclude for second-line use and 86% of those enrolled were Asian, which is the ethnic composition of the trial and not a statement about who the drug suits. Below the four cards, a cell records that these are not head-to-head comparisons: the guideline admits in so many words that no randomised trial has ever compared the two first-line drugs directly, its judgement being that a progressing patient with no matched target should have one of the two and that in most cases lenvatinib is preferred, a strong recommendation with high certainty, while cabozantinib is for patients who have progressed on one of those drugs, also strong with high certainty - a sequence and not a ranking. A further cell covers redifferentiation: the 2025 International Thyroid Oncology Group statement reports restoration of iodine uptake ranging from 33% to 95% between trials and tumour response from 11% to 80%, with wide differences in eligibility, timing, radioiodine activity and dosimetry, and the sentence that matters most is "Randomised studies are missing"; the only completed phase III was not asking about salvage at all, ASTRA having enrolled high-risk postoperative patients who were not genomically selected, randomised 233 of them and found complete remission at eighteen months in 40% against 38%, odds ratio 1.07 (95% confidence interval 0.61 to 1.87), a negative result. The right column closes by stating that the Taiwan part is not on this figure: whether a drug is licensed, whether it is listed by the National Health Insurance, and whether the reimbursement rules name this cancer and these conditions are three separate questions with three different answers, and running them together goes wrong every time; this figure does not say which drug is reimbursed in Taiwan for which thyroid cancer, and the rules are transcribed verbatim in the sister article, "How this goes in Taiwan". A vertical dashed rule separates the two columns and no arrow anywhere on the figure joins a criterion on the left to a drug on the right. The figure ends with a red-bordered block headed "This figure will not turn four trials into a league table", holding four statements: the four cells are drawn on one scale so that the gap between the two bars within each cell can be seen, not so that one drug's bar can be compared with another's, because the populations, the lines of therapy and the control arms all differ; every confidence interval is printed with its level, and intervals at 99%, 96% and 95% cannot have their widths compared in the same sentence; what these drugs buy is time with the disease held down rather than a cure, and on whether they make people live longer not one of the four trials above was designed to answer that question - overall survival is a secondary or exploratory endpoint in all four and all four let the placebo arm cross over after progressing, which by itself blurs the endpoint; one at a time, sorafenib showed no significant difference (0.80, 0.54 to 1.19), cabozantinib's 0.76 (0.45 to 1.31) is likewise not significant, the interim analysis of dabrafenib plus trametinib did not reach significance (0.66, 0.36 to 1.19) and that trial is still running, and lenvatinib published no overall-survival hazard ratio or test at all, so that none of them proved a benefit in overall survival, which is not the same sentence as "there is no benefit in overall survival"; and redifferentiation has no randomised evidence, the one completed phase III was negative, and it was not even asking about salvage. A closing cell carries three sentences to ask before a drug is started: on which criterion was I judged refractory to radioiodine; are my lesions growing now and by how much since last time; and if three months of this does not hold the disease down, what is our next step.

g.text: HOW "REFRACTORY" IS DEFINED - AND WHAT EACH TRIAL ACTUALLY MEASURED
The criteria on the left, the trials on the right, and not
every interval is 95%
"Radioiodine is not working for you" is a criterion with a written form. The left column is that criterion and where the guideline
puts it; the right column is what each of four trials enrolled, what the median progression-free survival was, and what the
hazard ratio was.
Every hazard ratio here is printed with the level of its confidence interval, because they are not all 95%. Which drug is
reimbursed in Taiwan for which thyroid cancer is not on this figure.
Nothing in the left column carries an evidence grade
The two gates are listed by the guideline as good practice, which it does not grade; the criteria themselves sit in the discussion paragraph beneath them
and carry no recommendation strength at all.
The guideline also says these criteria will go on changing.
Left column - how "refractory" is decided
Two gates first, and only then the criteria themselves.
Right column - four trials: how many, median
progression-free survival, hazard ratio
The bars are median progression-free survival in months, drug above and control
below, drawn on one common scale; but the populations, the lines of therapy and the
control arms differ, so bar length is not a conclusion that can be compared between
cells.
The two gates
Good practice, which the guideline does not grade
Without radioiodine, no diagnosis of refractory
A patient who has never had ablative or therapeutic radioiodine cannot
be diagnosed as refractory to it; those who qualify should have it first,
because that is how the answer is found.
Once refractory, no further empiric radioiodine
A patient already judged refractory should not be given empiric
radioiodine again; other treatments are to be considered.
Strong criteria: two
Visible, but takes up no iodine
A lesion visible on imaging or PET with no iodine uptake on the
post-therapy scan.
Treated, and progressing quickly
Progression within six months of one appropriately dosed radioiodine
treatment where the post-therapy scan did show uptake.
Supportive criteria: two
No uptake on the diagnostic scan
No uptake on the diagnostic scan while the lesion is visible on imaging.
This predicts a poorer response, but some such patients still have a
positive post-therapy scan.
Only some lesions take up iodine
This does not rule radioiodine out, but radioiodine alone is not enough.
Refractory does not mean a short time left
The guideline says in the same section that some patients die within
three to five years, and that others survive a long time with stable or
extremely slowly progressive disease.
So the first step after "refractory" is often not a drug at all: patients
who are asymptomatic, stable or barely progressing, or who carry
significant comorbidity, may be imaged every three to twelve months
on suppressive thyroid hormone therapy (conditional recommendation,
low certainty).
The threshold for starting a drug is imaging, not a blood test
The guideline requires visible progression of lesions on imaging before
systemic therapy is started, not a blood curve climbing upwards.
A rising thyroglobulin on its own is written down as not constituting a
reason to start systemic therapy.
The trials below enrolled people with progression on imaging in the first
place. Applying their conclusions to a different group buys none of the result
and all of the side effects.
Test the tumour tissue for biomarkers before systemic
therapy starts
A strong recommendation with moderate certainty. The drugs chosen by
genotype work well but rest on very few patients; those numbers are in the
article, and this figure carries only the phase III trials.
Read this cell carefully: not every interval is 95%
Hazard ratio 0.21 for lenvatinib
99% confidence interval
Response rate for cabozantinib (interim
analysis)
99% confidence interval
Progression-free survival hazard ratio
0.22 for cabozantinib
96% confidence interval
Hazard ratios in the sorafenib and BRAF
phase III trials
95% confidence interval
When the levels differ, the widths of the intervals cannot be read in the same
sentence. And if you see "median progression-free survival not reached" for
cabozantinib, that is the older wording from the interim analysis; the 2022
extended analysis is the one to use.
The lenvatinib phase III
392 patients with radioiodine-refractory, progressive differentiated thyroid cancer (261
on drug, 131 on placebo)
Drug
18.3 months
Placebo
3.6 months
Hazard ratio 0.21 (0.14 to 0.31)
99% confidence interval
Response 64.8% (4 of them complete) against 1.5%. On overall survival: this trial
published no overall-survival hazard ratio or test at all, only that median
overall survival had not been reached in either arm.
The cost: discontinuation for adverse events 14.2% against 2.3%; of 20 deaths
during treatment, 6 were judged drug-related; hypertension, diarrhoea,
fatigue, loss of appetite and weight loss each above four in ten.
The sorafenib phase III
417 patients (207 on drug, 210 on placebo), radioiodine-refractory, locally advanced or
metastatic and progressing
Drug
10.8 months
Placebo
5.8 months
Hazard ratio 0.59 (0.45 to 0.76)
95% confidence interval
Overall survival showed no significant difference, hazard ratio 0.80 (0.54 to
1.19); 71.4% of the placebo arm crossed over to the drug after progressing,
and the authors write that the overall-survival result may be confounded by it.
Response 12.2% (24/196), all of them partial. Dose interruption 66.2%, reduction
64.3%, discontinuation for adverse events 18.8%; serious adverse events 37.2%
against 26.3%.
The cabozantinib phase III (2022 extended analysis)
258 randomised, median follow-up 10.1 months; used in patients who progressed on one
of the drugs above
Drug
11.0 months
Control
1.9 months
Hazard ratio 0.22 (0.15 to 0.32)
96% confidence interval
The interval around the median of 11.0 months is a 96% confidence interval of
7.4 to 13.8. Response 11.0% (95% confidence interval 6.9 to 16.9) against 0;
grade 3 or 4 adverse events 62% against 28%. The overall-survival hazard
ratio of 0.76 (0.45 to 1.31) is likewise not significant, and the authors write that
crossover will confound future analyses of overall survival.
In the interim analysis (187 patients) the response rate was 10/67 among the
first 100 randomised (15%, 99% confidence interval 5.8 to 29.3) against 0/33,
which did not meet the prespecified threshold for significance.
The BRAF phase III, which read out after the guideline was
written
153 previously treated patients with BRAF V600E-positive, radioiodine-refractory
differentiated thyroid cancer, randomised 101 to 52
Drug
12.8 months
Control
3.7 months
Stratified hazard ratio 0.38 (0.25 to 0.57)
95% confidence interval
The interval around the median of 12.8 months is a 95% confidence interval of
10.2 to 21.2. Response 57% against 4%.
The interim analysis of overall survival has not reached significance
(stratified hazard ratio 0.66, 0.36 to 1.19), and that trial is still running. The
authors conclude for second-line use; 86% of those enrolled were Asian, which
is the ethnic composition of the trial and not a statement about who the drug
suits.
These four trials are not head-to-head comparisons
The guideline admits in so many words that no randomised trial has
ever compared the two first-line drugs directly. Its judgement is that a
progressing patient with no matched target should have one of the two,
and that in most cases lenvatinib is preferred (strong recommendation,
high certainty).
Cabozantinib is for patients who have progressed on one of those
drugs (strong recommendation, high certainty). That is a sequence, not
a ranking.
Redifferentiation: no randomised evidence, and the one phase
III was negative
The 2025 International Thyroid Oncology Group statement is candid:
restoration of iodine uptake ranged from 33% to 95% between trials and tumour
response from 11% to 80%, while the trials differ widely in eligibility, timing,
radioiodine activity and dosimetry; and the sentence that matters most is
"Randomised studies are missing".
The only completed phase III was not asking about salvage at all: ASTRA
enrolled high-risk postoperative patients who were not genomically selected,
randomised 233 of them, and found complete remission at eighteen months in
40% against 38%, odds ratio 1.07 (95% confidence interval 0.61 to 1.87) -
negative.
The Taiwan part is not on this figure
Whether a drug is licensed, whether it is listed by the National Health
Insurance, and whether the reimbursement rules name this cancer and these
conditions are three separate questions with three different answers, and
running them together goes wrong every time.
This figure does not say which drug is reimbursed in Taiwan for which
thyroid cancer. The rules are transcribed verbatim in the sister article, "How
this goes in Taiwan".
This figure will not turn four trials into a league table
The four cells are drawn on one scale so that you can see how far apart the two bars within each cell are, not so that you can compare the length of one
drug's bar with another's. The populations, the lines of therapy and the control arms all differ, and the guideline itself says no randomised trial has
ever compared them directly.
Every confidence interval is printed with its level. Intervals at 99%, 96% and 95% cannot have their widths compared in the same sentence.
What these drugs buy is time with the disease held down, not a cure. On whether they make people live longer, not one of the four trials above was
designed to answer that question: overall survival is a secondary or exploratory endpoint in all four, and all four let the placebo arm cross over to the
drug after progressing, which by itself blurs that endpoint. One at a time: sorafenib showed no significant difference (0.80, 0.54 to 1.19); cabozantinib's
0.76 (0.45 to 1.31) is likewise not significant; the interim analysis of dabrafenib plus trametinib did not reach significance (0.66, 0.36 to 1.19) and that
trial is still running; and lenvatinib published no overall-survival hazard ratio or test at all. None of them proved a benefit in overall survival - which is
not the same sentence as "there is no benefit in overall survival", and the second sentence is not written here.
Redifferentiation has no randomised evidence, the one completed phase III was negative, and it was not even asking about salvage.
Three sentences to ask before a drug is started
"On which criterion was I judged refractory to radioiodine?"
"Are my lesions growing now, and by how much since last time?"
"If three months of this does not hold the disease down, what is our next step?"
Schematic, redrawn from the 2025 American Thyroid Association guidelines for differentiated thyroid cancer, the two first-line phase III trials of lenvatinib and
sorafenib, the interim and 2022 extended analyses of the cabozantinib phase III, the BRAF phase III reported in 2026, the 2025 International Thyroid Oncology Group
statement on redifferentiation and the ASTRA trial; not reproduced from the figures of the original papers. The cohorts, designs and endpoints of the underlying
studies differ, so the data points must not be compared directly.
